props.title: Sleeper
props.initialSlug: Man wakes in 2173, fights dystopian future with wit

sections.content: Woody Allen's sci-fi comedy Sleeper (1973) brilliantly merges slapstick with dystopian satire, drawing heavily from Buster Keaton and Charlie Chaplin's physical comedy traditions. Allen plays Miles Monroe, a health food store owner cryogenically frozen in 1973 who awakens 200 years later in a totalitarian future. The film's retro-futuristic aesthetic - with its gleaming white architecture and bizarre gadgets - both parodies and pays homage to serious sci-fi films like 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) and THX 1138 (1971). Allen's trademark neurotic humor finds fresh ground in the absurdist future setting.

sections.content: The 1970s marked a pivotal shift in sci-fi comedy, with films daring to merge social commentary with outright farce. While Sleeper lampooned contemporary health fads and political paranoia, films like The Bed Sitting Room (1969) and A Boy and His Dog (1975) used pitch-black humor to process Cold War anxieties. Allen's film stands out for maintaining a lighter touch while still embedding sharp criticism of authority, conformity, and technological dependence.

The film's influence echoes through later sci-fi comedies like Brazil (1985), Back to the Future (1985), and Idiocracy (2006), all of which use fish-out-of-water protagonists to critique their present through imagined futures. Sleeper's combination of physical comedy and futuristic satire created a template for blending genres that remains relevant, seen in films like Wall-E (2008) and Her (2013). sections.content: Sleeper's masterful physical comedy sequences - particularly the scene with the giant banana peel and the malfunctioning robot butler - demonstrate how sci-fi settings can enhance rather than inhibit slapstick. This tradition continues in films like The Fifth Element (1997) and Galaxy Quest (1999), where futuristic environments become playgrounds for physical humor. Allen's performance specifically channels silent film techniques, proving their timeless appeal even in advanced technological settings.
